title: Payment Demand Letter | Free Word Template
description: Free payment demand letter: formal demand for unpaid money before legal action or collections.
lead: A formal letter demanding payment of an overdue amount (unpaid invoice, loan, rent or damages) stating what is owed, by when, and what happens if not paid.
introParagraphs: A payment demand letter (or demand for payment) is a formal written request for money owed — an unpaid invoice, personal loan, security deposit refund, or damages. It states the amount owed, the basis, a deadline, and consequences if not paid (collections, small claims or lawsuit).

A well-drafted demand letter is often the first thing a small-claims judge asks for. Send it via certified mail with return receipt (and email) so you have proof the other side received it. Keep a copy.
bullets: Your details and theirs
Your name/company, address and contact; recipient name/company and address; date of letter.
Amount owed
Total amount due, including any interest, late fees or costs, with a breakdown.
Basis of the debt
What the money is for (unpaid invoice #X dated Y, personal loan on date Z, damages from incident on date) with attached copies of invoices/contracts.
Deadline and payment method
Deadline for payment (typically 14-30 days) and how/where to pay.
Consequences
Statement of next steps if not paid by the deadline (small claims court, collections attorney, eviction) — without threatening criminal action.
howTo: Gather documentation
Pull the invoice, contract, emails and any proof of delivery/payment attempts to attach.
State the facts calmly
Do not editorialise or threaten — state amount owed, what it is for, and deadline plainly.
Calculate the total correctly
Include interest/late fees only if allowed by contract or law; show a breakdown.
Set a clear deadline
Give enough time for response (14-30 days is typical) and specify the payment method/address.
Deliver with proof
Send by certified mail (return receipt) and email; keep a signed copy and tracking receipt.
related: Demand to stop non-monetary harmful conduct.
Document the loan if you are lending money.
Friendlier reminder before a formal demand.
faq: Is a demand letter required before suing?
Often not legally required, but small claims courts and attorneys strongly recommend (and in some jurisdictions expect) a written demand before filing.
Should I send by email or mail?
Both — email for speed, certified mail for proof of receipt. Certified mail return receipt is the strongest evidence.
Can I add interest?
Only if the contract or a state statute allows it; in many states you can add post-judgment interest, but pre-judgment interest must be contractual.
What if they ignore it?
You can proceed to small claims court, collections, or hire an attorney based on the amount and merits.
Do I need a lawyer?
You can write one yourself; a lawyer adds weight for larger amounts or if you expect litigation.

title: Payment Reminder Letter | Free Word Template
description: Free payment reminder letter: polite nudge for an overdue invoice before sending a formal demand.
lead: A friendly reminder that a payment is overdue — sent a few days after the due date before escalating to a formal demand, with invoice details and how to pay.
introParagraphs: A payment reminder letter (or friendly reminder email) is sent shortly after an invoice becomes overdue. It is more polite than a demand letter, assumes the late payment may be an oversight, and gives the client an easy way to pay.
Send the first reminder 3-7 days after the due date, a firmer one at 14-30 days, and a formal demand letter at 30+ days. Most late invoices are paid after the second reminder.
bullets: Your and client details
Your name/company, client name/company, date of the reminder.
Invoice details
Invoice number, original invoice date, due date, amount due and the services/products it covers.
Payment methods
How to pay (bank transfer, card, cheque, link), payment details/link and who to contact with issues.
Late fees (optional)
Reminder of any contractual late fee, phrased neutrally.
Tone appropriate to lateness
Friendly for 7-day reminders; firmer for 30-day reminders; attach the original invoice.
howTo: Wait a few days
Send the first reminder 3-7 days after the due date — the client may simply have forgotten.
Be polite and brief
Assume good faith; state the invoice number, amount and how to pay.
Attach the invoice again
Clients often lose the original; re-attaching it reduces friction to pay.
Offer a quick conversation
Invite them to contact you if there is a problem or dispute — resolving it early saves escalation.
Escalate if needed
If no response after 14-30 days, send a firmer reminder and then a formal demand letter.
related: Formal demand when reminders are ignored.
Send a clear invoice in the first place.
If the client is disputing an amount, issue a credit note for the disputed portion.
faq: How many reminders before a demand?
Typically 2-3: a friendly reminder at 7 days, a firmer one at 14-21 days, then a demand letter at 30 days.
Can I charge late fees on reminders?
Only if they were in the original contract/terms and comply with state usury laws.
Is email enough?
For early reminders, yes; switch to certified mail once you escalate to a demand letter.
Should I call too?
A quick follow-up call after the email can resolve disputes quickly and preserves the relationship.
What if they dispute the invoice?
Pause collection, ask what they dispute in writing, and try to resolve — you cannot demand payment for a genuinely disputed amount without going to court.

title: Liability Waiver | Free Word Template
description: Free liability waiver (release of liability): protect your business from injury or damage claims before an activity.
lead: A release of liability signed by a participant (or parent/guardian) acknowledging the risks of an activity and waiving the right to sue the organiser for ordinary negligence.
introParagraphs: A liability waiver (or release of liability, assumption of risk, hold-harmless) is signed before an activity (fitness class, event, rental, tour, sport) by the participant. It acknowledges the risks and agrees not to hold the organiser liable for injury or damage from ordinary negligence.

Waivers do not protect you from gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct or certain statutory claims — and their enforceability varies significantly by state and activity. Have an attorney review your waiver, especially for high-risk activities or minors.
bullets: Organiser and participant
Business/organiser name and contact; participant name, address, phone and email; emergency contact.
Activity and risks
Description of the activity and the inherent risks involved (be specific — e.g. falling, collision, equipment failure, drowning).
Assumption of risk
Statement that the participant understands and voluntarily assumes the risks.
Release of liability
Participant waives, releases and discharges the organiser from claims arising from ordinary negligence, to the fullest extent permitted by law.
Other clauses
Indemnification, medical consent (authorising emergency treatment), governing law, severability, photo release if applicable, and parent/guardian signature for minors.
howTo: Identify the real risks
List the specific risks of your activity — generic 'all risks' language is weaker than specific risks.
Make it conspicuous
Use clear language, bold the release/assumption sections, and do not bury the waiver in small print.
Separate from registration
Have participants sign the waiver as a standalone document (or clearly marked section) before the activity begins.
Get it signed in advance
Have the participant sign (or parent/guardian for minors) before they start the activity — never after an injury.
Keep signed copies
File signed waivers securely (digital or paper) for at least the statute-of-limitations period (often 2-3 years for injury claims).
related: Settlement release after a dispute or incident.
Image/likeness release often bundled with activity waivers.
Event-client contract that usually references attendee waivers.
faq: Are liability waivers enforceable?
For ordinary negligence, in most states yes if written clearly and signed knowingly; they do not cover gross negligence or intentional harm.
Can a parent waive a minor's claims?
Many states will not enforce a parent pre-injury waiver against a minor injury claim, though some allow it; consult local counsel.
Do I need one for every activity?
Use one for any activity with physical risk (sports, fitness, outdoor activities, equipment rentals, events).
Does it replace insurance?
No — waivers are one layer; carry appropriate general liability/professional insurance.
Do digital signatures work?
Yes, as long as the signer is clearly identified and the waiver language is presented conspicuously before signature.

title: Hold Harmless Agreement | Free Word Template
description: Free hold harmless agreement: one party agrees to protect the other from specified claims, losses or lawsuits.
lead: An agreement where one party (indemnitor) agrees to indemnify, defend and hold the other (indemnitee) harmless from specified claims, losses, liabilities or lawsuits arising from an activity, contract or arrangement.
introParagraphs: A hold harmless agreement (or indemnity agreement) allocates risk between two parties: if something goes wrong, the indemnitor pays for losses, damages or legal costs instead of (or before) the indemnitee. Common in construction, events, vendor contracts, rentals and service agreements.

Indemnity clauses are heavily litigated. The scope, duty to defend, and limits on liability matter enormously; many states restrict indemnification for one's own negligence unless the contract says so clearly and conspicuously.
bullets: Parties
Indemnitor (party taking on liability) and indemnitee (party being protected); names, addresses and signing authority.
Activity/contract covered
Specific activity, project, event or contract the indemnity applies to, and the time period.
Scope of indemnity
What losses are covered: third-party claims, bodily injury, property damage, attorney fees, fines; whether negligence of the indemnitee is covered; and any limits.
Duty to defend
Whether the indemnitor must provide a defence (and pick counsel) or just reimburse after a loss.
Insurance and limits
Required insurance (general liability, workers comp, professional) with named additional insured; certificate of insurance; any cap on liability.
howTo: Define the risk clearly
Specify what is and is not covered; vague 'all claims' language is harder to enforce.
Match the insurance requirement
Require insurance limits that back the indemnity; ask for a certificate naming you as additional insured.
Be explicit about negligence
If you want indemnity for your own partial negligence, most states require clear 'including negligence of indemnitee' language.
Add defence duty
Make the indemnitor defend you from the start of a claim (not just pay after judgment); this is a key practical protection.
Have counsel review
Indemnity is highly state-specific — have a local attorney review for enforceability before signing.
related: Participant-facing waiver signed before an activity.
Release of claims after a dispute settles.
Service contracts often contain mutual hold-harmless clauses.
Clients typically indemnify organisers for event-specific risks.
faq: Is hold harmless the same as indemnity?
Often used interchangeably; technically 'hold harmless' protects against loss, 'indemnify' reimburses after loss — but most contracts use both.
Can I indemnify myself from my own negligence?
Most states allow it only if the contract says so clearly and conspicuously; some states ban it entirely for certain industries (e.g. construction).
Does it replace insurance?
No — an indemnity without insurance backing is only as strong as the indemnitor ability to pay; always require matching insurance.
Mutual or one-way?
Either — two businesses contracting often indemnify each other; a venue will usually require one-way indemnity from the renter.
Do I need a separate agreement?
Short-form indemnity can be a clause in a larger contract; standalone agreements are common for one-off events or high-risk activities.

title: Gift Letter | Free Word Template
description: Free gift letter: confirm that money gifted to a homebuyer is a true gift with no repayment expected.
lead: A letter from a donor to a borrower (and their lender) confirming that a sum of money given for a down payment is a true gift — not a loan that has to be repaid.
introParagraphs: A gift letter is required by mortgage lenders when part (or all) of a borrower down payment is being given by a family member or other donor. It confirms the money is a gift with no expectation of repayment, and states the donor relationship, the amount, and the source of funds.

Lenders require gift letters to ensure that gifted funds are not a hidden loan that would affect the borrower debt-to-income ratio. The donor typically needs to show proof of funds (bank statements) and a transfer paper trail.
bullets: Donor and borrower
Donor full name, address, phone; borrower name(s); relationship between donor and borrower.
Gift details
Amount of the gift, date transferred (or to be transferred), and address of the property being purchased.
No-repayment statement
Clear statement that the money is a gift and no repayment is expected or implied.
Source of funds
Account the money came from (bank, institution) — lender may require statements.
Signatures
Donor and borrower signatures, date; some lenders require notarisation.
howTo: Check lender requirements
Ask your lender for their required format; many have their own template.
Fill out before transfer
Draft and sign the letter before (or with) the wire transfer so the paper trail is clean.
Document the transfer
Keep a copy of the wire/cheque and a gift receipt so the lender can trace the funds.
Provide donor bank statements if asked
Lenders often want to see the donor ability to give and the withdrawal from their account.
Sign and deliver
Donor signs, borrower signs, submit to the loan officer before underwriting.
related: Use a promissory note if the money IS a loan rather than a gift.
Formal loan contract with interest and repayment terms.
Confirm lender-required format before using a generic template.
A signed receipt helps document the transfer.
faq: Who can give a gift for a mortgage?
Typically immediate family (parents, grandparents, siblings, spouses); some loans allow gifts from close friends, employers or charities.
Is a gift letter legally binding?
It is a signed statement to the lender — lying (claiming a gift when it is a loan) is mortgage fraud.
Do I have to pay tax on a gifted down payment?
In the US the donor typically pays gift tax if over the annual exclusion (currently $18,000 per person per year, 2024); the recipient usually does not pay tax.
Do I need proof of the transfer?
Yes — lenders want to see the wire/cheque and the money landing in your account before closing.
Can the donor take the money back?
Once gifted and documented, no — that would be a loan, not a gift, and would change the loan picture.
